#143721. Harvard’s tiny UV light chip could help shrink quantum computers

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1192 w)
📖 Baca
Hardware & Chips ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Harvard’s tiny UV light chip could help shrink quantum computers

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1192 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that ultraviolet (UV) light is already essential to a wide range of modern technologies.
  • However, shrinking UV light sources to fit on a chip has presented a significant engineering challenge.
  • Now, a Harvard-led research team has demonstrated a microscopic photonic device that produces approximately 120 times more UV power than previous comparable devices.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that ultraviolet (UV) light is already essential to a wide range of modern technologies. Beyond its natural presence in sunlight, it is used to disinfect surfaces, make biological materials fluoresce, and manufacture computer chips through a process called photolithography. In the future, microscopic sources of UV light built directly into photonic chips could enable smaller quantum computers, ultra-precise atomic clocks, and other advanced technologies.

However, shrinking UV light sources to fit on a chip has presented a significant engineering challenge. Ultraviolet light rapidly loses power as it travels through optical waveguides, the tiny channels that carry light across a chip. This limitation has made it extremely difficult to develop compact UV sources with enough power for practical applications.

Now, a Harvard-led research team has demonstrated a microscopic photonic device that produces approximately 120 times more UV power than previous comparable devices. The researchers, working in the laboratory of Marko Lončar, the Tiantsai Lin Professor of Electrical Engineering, achieved the breakthrough using a widely studied material called thin-film lithium niobate.

Published in Nature Communications, the findings establish lithium niobate as a promising platform for generating powerful ultraviolet light in compact devices while minimizing optical losses.

Turning Red Light Into Ultraviolet Light.

Rather than trying to deliver ultraviolet light directly through microscopic channels, the researchers designed a device that generates UV light from red light within the chip itself.

The approach relies on a process known as frequency upconversion. Inside the lithium niobate crystal, two photons of red light combine to produce a single ultraviolet photon with higher energy. Lithium niobate is particularly well suited to this process because of its exceptional ability to convert light from one frequency to another.

"Our group is perhaps best known for utilizing lithium niobate for photonic devices that operate at longer, infrared wavelengths -- closer to the realm of telecommunications signals," Lončar said.

However, the team found that this transparent crystalline material, which has become increasingly important in integrated photonics, can also support light sources and guide light at much shorter wavelengths, including those in the ultraviolet range.

"When people think about [thin-film lithium niobate], they don't think of it as a UV material, but we show that it is," said co-first author Kees Franken, former research fellow in the Lončar lab. "We also show that there are some other nonlinear effects happening that we don't fully understand yet.".

A Newly introduced Technique Overcomes a Major Engineering Barrier.

The device uses optical waveguides, microscopic channels etched into the lithium niobate film that direct light through the chip in much the same way electrical wires carry current.

According to recent reports, for red light to be efficiently converted into ultraviolet light, the orientation of regions within the crystal must be repeatedly reversed at precisely controlled intervals along the waveguide. This manufacturing process, called poling, is a specialized technique used in nonlinear optics.

One of the biggest challenges has been creating these patterns with accuracy at scales smaller than a micrometer across devices that extend for centimeters.

In a recent development, previous manufacturing methods required researchers to make an undesirable compromise. Poling the entire film before forming the waveguides made it difficult to correct manufacturing imperfections. Alternatively, creating the waveguides first reduced conversion efficiency because the electrodes were positioned too far away, allowing only part of the film to be successfully poled.

To eliminate this tradeoff, the Harvard team developed a technique they call "sidewall poling.".

Precision Engineering Dramatically Improves Light Conversion.

Sources indicate that instead of positioning the electrodes exclusively above the lithium niobate film, the researchers placed precisely patterned metal structures resembling tiny fingers directly alongside the etched waveguide. During fabrication, they applied a small voltage to permanently reverse the orientation of the crystal domains in a carefully controlled pattern.

"The key idea was: could we just put the electrodes directly on the waveguide?" said co-first author and former graduate student Soumya Ghosh. "It's a high-precision fabrication process to position the electrodes but requiring about 50-nanometer accuracy.".

This arrangement enabled the researchers to reverse the crystal domains throughout the entire cross section of the waveguide, allowing light traveling through the material to undergo much more efficient frequency conversion.

In a recent development, the team could also fine-tune the spacing of the reversed crystal regions along the device. By incorporating existing "adapted poling" techniques previously developed in Lončar's laboratory and elsewhere, the researchers compensated for variations in the thickness of the lithium niobate film and the shape of the waveguide.

A 120-Fold Increase in Ultraviolet Power.

It has been revealed that the resulting device generated 4.2 milliwatts of ultraviolet power directly on the chip at a wavelength of 390 nanometers. That represents approximately 120 times the output power achieved by the best previous thin-film lithium niobate devices operating in this wavelength range.

Earlier experiments using the material generated only tens of microwatts of UV power. Although those results demonstrated that the approach was scientifically feasible, the output was too low to support practical applications.

Recent findings suggest that the substantial increase in power could be particularly valuable for trapped-ion quantum computers. These machines use electrically charged atoms to store and process quantum information. Many of the specific atomic energy transitions required to operate them involve light in the near-ultraviolet portion of the spectrum.

"If you want a scalable quantum computer that isn't the size of a truck, you need to scale everything down to the chip level, and this includes the light sources," Franken stated.

In a recent development, the technology could also benefit ultra-precise atomic clocks and environmental monitoring systems. According to the researchers, the same range of ultraviolet wavelengths is well suited to compact sensors designed to closely monitor greenhouse gases and other atmospheric pollutants.

Franken and Ghosh attribute the breakthrough partly to the collaborative structure of Lončar's laboratory, where researchers carry out every stage of device development in one place, including theoretical research, engineering design, cleanroom fabrication, and optical testing.

"The hands-on intuition that we gained for how to make a device, while also keeping the zoomed-out view of what this device is for, and how we were going to characterize it -- that's a big part of what enabled this project for us," Ghosh remarked.

"Milliwatt-level UV generation using sidewall poled lithium niobate" was further co-authored by C.C. Rodrigues, J. Yang, C.J. Xin, S. Lu, D. Witt, G. Joe, G.S. Wiederhecker, and K.-J. Boller.

It has been revealed that U.S. federal funding for the project came from the following sources: Department of the Air Force grant No. FA9453-23-C-A039; Office of Naval Research grant No. N00014-22-C-1041/VAS-21-0001; NASA grant No. 80NSSC22K0262 and 80NSSC23PB442; and National Science Foundation grants ERC EEC-1941583 and OMA-2137723.

Materials provided by Harvard John A. Paulson School of Engineering and Applied Sciences. Original written by Anne J. Manning. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The true box office winner of Dunesday has been predicted by the Nielsen ratings, and it's none other than Avengers: Doomsday.

Per Deadline, NRG (National Research Group, owned by Nielsen) predicts that Doomsday will bring in $270 million at the global box office during its opening weekend. Dune 3 is predicted to bring in $75 million.

This is the highest projection NRG has ever recorded, with Spider-Man: Brand New Day being the second-highest. To date, Avengers: Endgame now holds the record second-highest opening weekend for any movie ever at $357.1M, having been beat out by Spider-Man: Brand New Day's $360 million.

Industry observers note that avengers: Doomsday tickets went on sale back in July for the special Infinity Vision screenings. It's worth noting that 60,000 more tickets were sold for the early Thursday screenings following the VisionQuest finale, which teases the return of Wanda Maximoff aka the Scarlet Witch. Wanda will indeed return in Doomsday, but she won't be, uh, herself... if you catch my drift.

Dune 3 tickets have been a bit of a nightmare for fans as they sold out almost immediately back in April, and then crashed several movie theater apps when more tickets were released back in August. Oh, and, when tickets did sell out in April... people started reselling them for up to $1000. The people yearn for sand.

According to recent reports, avengers: Doomsday and Dune 3 hit theaters on December 18. For more on the MCU, check out our guide to the Marvel timeline and how to watch the Marvel movies in order.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Team Ninja continues to work on Nioh 3.
  • Today’s patch, version 1.04, is a major one, coming in at well over 1GB.
  • Industry observers note that to begin with, this is the patch that adds the promised free armour sets for both Ninja, and Samurai.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Team Ninja continues to work on Nioh 3. The developer has been releasing regular updates for the action RPG since its launch in early February. Earlier patches have addressed major bugs like healing item use inconsistencies, and more have arrived since to tackle various balance and loot-related issues.

Today’s patch, version 1.04, is a major one, coming in at well over 1GB. There’s plenty here worth getting excited about, so let’s dig in.

Industry observers note that to begin with, this is the patch that adds the promised free armour sets for both Ninja, and Samurai. When Nioh 3 reached one million sales, Team Ninja mentioned it would gift every player the Thunderous set in celebration, and the set’s two variants are now available in-game.

The more interesting side of the patch is, unsurprisingly, its change log. There appears to be a focus on online co-op and AI summons in this one, with various tweaks to the make the process more rewarding, and, in some cases, worthwhile.

The amount of Glory obtained when you complete a mission in multiplayer has been increased, regardless of which player was the host. The other major change mainly affects AI Benevolent Grave summons, making it so bosses will no longer target a single player for almost the entirety of the fight.

While summoning AI helpers has always been useful in Nioh 3, they didn’t always help in boss fights, specifically because the boss tended to focus on the player who summoned them, leaving the AI to run around eating AoE hits before dying.

It has been revealed that patch 1.04 makes a couple of welcome gameplay tweaks to the feel of combat. Ninjutsu, and Onmyo Magic will now hit their targets more consistently in situations where there’s a difference in elevation between the player and the enemy.

Sources indicate that in the same vein, you’ll now be able to attack (quick/strong) right after jumping, which removes the pause that previously buffered the attack instead. This could mean even more air combos that don’t specifically require Martial Arts.

You can look forward to a couple of quality of life tweaks in this patch, too, such as the change that allows the game to automatically send any Sudama Soul Cores dropped by merchants to your item box. This happens from the second one onwards, which means you won’t have to pick half a dozen each time you go to sell a batch of items.

Speaking of the item box, the limit of forging materials has been increased for some of them. If you’ve been running Battle Scroll missions and Expeditions for gear, you’ll be happy to know that you can now exit the session from the main menu directly.

There’s plenty more to patch 1.04, including fixes and balance tweaks for several weapons, such as Samurai dual swords, odachi, and more for a few Ninja weapons, too. The patch also brings several bug fixes to the game.

You can read the full set of patch notes on Steam.

GTA 6 developers at Rockstar are worried about being laid off after shipping "the biggest game of all time"

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (439 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Eurogamer

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that rockstar has successfully shipped Grand Theft Auto 6, after years of work and more than a billion dollars spent.
  • But that may not be enough to prevent layoffs at Rockstar, some people working within the studio fear.
  • "After the massive day, we have had no indication that layoffs are coming, but it's hard not to worry about what the future holds," Uriarte wrote.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that rockstar has successfully shipped Grand Theft Auto 6, after years of work and more than a billion dollars spent. GTA 6 is already one of the highest-rated games ever - Eurogamer awarded it five stars in our GTA 6 review - and it's expected to be among the most successful, best-selling games ever.

But that may not be enough to prevent layoffs at Rockstar, some people working within the studio fear. Nestor Uriarte, an animation programmer at Rockstar North, wrote about their concern for their job and those of their colleagues in an article on The Guardian.

"After the massive day, we have had no indication that layoffs are coming, but it's hard not to worry about what the future holds," Uriarte wrote. "It says a lot about the industry that even my colleagues and I, working on the biggest game of all time, are worried about getting laid off. But the truth is that workers across the sector are helpless to resist the waves of redundancies crashing around us, until we get organised.".

Uriarte's piece comes as Rockstar staff's efforts to establish a union reach a critical point. A tribunal between the studio and fired IWBG union members just concluded, though the verdict may not arrive for many weeks or months.

Rockstar's UK studios are at the moment voting on recognising an official Rockstar workers union. Uriarte is in support of it and has urged colleagues to vote in favour of it. Results of that vote are expected today.

"Winning union recognition would be a huge step forward in securing a meaningful say over our conditions at Rockstar, but its significance would reach far beyond that," Uriarte pointed out.

"As one of the biggest and most influential game studios in the world, what happens here could open the door for other workers across the UK to imagine an alternative future for the industry - one in which workers' voices are taken into account more.".

Across its 12 offices around the world, Rockstar's headcount grew to 4,711 during GTA 6's development - double its size when it released Red Dead Redemption 2.

As popular and profitable as Rockstar's games are, the firm has initiated layoffs in the past after shipping a major project. While there's no way of knowing whether the same is going to happen for GTA 6, the justifiable concerns - given the current state of the industry - are there. According to the ASGC Games Industry Layoffs Tracker, more than 12,000 developers have lost their jobs this year so far, up from more than 9,000 people last year.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Sims 4 will soon get a latest update to resolve a number of concerns, some of which have long caused headaches for players. The latest update will arrive March 17 on PC and Mac, followed by PlayStation and Xbox at an unspecified time later.

Outside of the fixes themselves, the patch also makes good on the recent re-commitment to continue improving quality of life for players, so there’s plenty here longtime players will appreciate.

In the latest episode of The Sims 4’s Laundry List blog series, where the developer goes through the most reported problems with the game and how it intends to solve them, we got a rundown of what to expect from next week’s patch.

It has been revealed that you can look forward to five major fixes in this one, but arguably the most crucial is a change to how Sims determine who they speak with on a lot. This is especially relevant for public lots, where Sims would sometimes interrupt ongoing conversations by barging in and starting a conversation with your Sim.

Going forward, Sims will prioritise familiar Sims with whom they already have rapport, and be less likely to latch onto strangers. If you’ve witnessed a date your Sim was on get interrupted because of that, you’ll certainly appreciate the change.

Speaking of budding romance, Prom is coming back to in-game Calendars, and Sims can once again attend. Maxis mentioned this will work with new and existing saves, and that you should also expect Prom goals to be completable once again.

Pets and animals get some love in this patch, too. First, pets and horses will no longer get lost in Premade Households. The fix prevents that from happening in fresh saves, but if you already had that happen to you in your current save, it’ll still be there.

You may now also assign animals to an Animal Shed after moving your house to a newly introduced lot, so you hopefully won’t be confused as to why they’re stuck in your inventory. This fix applies to existing saves as well as new ones.

Lower down the list of urgent fixes is an revision that makes it so Sims’ eye blinking will show fully closed eyes for most interactions. The upcoming patch also comes with a host of Sims autonomy fixes, including one that prevents them from excessively flirting with each other.

Catch up on the full list at the link near the top of the page. And, in case you missed it, Maxis recently confirmed that The Sims 4 will soon get paid mods, something that many in the community are skeptical about.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the promise of user-generated content, this idea that you could host a platform that grows infinitely because the people that interact with it make things for it and you don't even have to pay anyone, is an alluring one. And its siren call has come for Dead by Daylight, as developer Behaviour Interactive have outlined the future of the game, which includes a way to make your own bits for the multiplayer horror game.

"What if you could create your own Dead by Daylight experiences?" explains a blog post recapping the plans for how the game is going to change. "As one of the most exciting updates coming in 2027, the Dead by Daylight Workshop will open the doors to user-created content in some incredible ways. From designing your own Maps and importing custom assets, to modifying game rules, objectives, and even creating entirely newly introduced modes, the possibilities are vast.".

Sources indicate that the post goes on to note that anything created in the workshop will "exist separately from all our classic modes, with dedicated creation tools and moderation provided to ensure experienced modders have everything they need to do their best work, and all submissions meet our official guidelines." I am always hesitant when it comes to UGC faff, because the ability to make your own custom Debbie Daylight maps might sound promising, but people do actually have to engage with them for the whole thing to work. It's just putting a hat on a hat!

Anyway, the workshop isn't the only thing Behaviour have in the works. For one, the game is getting a big visual overhaul. You can expect lighting improvements, more detailed assets and "tons of atmospheric touches," alongside revamps of particular maps like the Temple of Purgation and Backwater Swamp. Killers and survivors will be getting some TLC too by "improving character textures, proportions, hair, and animations to make them look and feel more lifelike. That includes updated character rigs, new motion capture, and new facial animation technology designed to better express a character’s fear, pain, and struggles over the course of a Trial.".

Beyond all of that, a dynamic weather system is coming to the game, meaning you'll now have to deal with the likes of rain, thunderstorms, snow and heavy wind, all of which can impact matches. Onboarding for newer folks should be getting some improvements too, with the addition of a "more cinematic introduction, clearer explanations and tutorials of game mechanics, and a more gradual introduction," to the game. All of this will be coming in one big update sometime in 2027, so, keep your eyes peeled for whenever that drops.

10 Elements Metroidvanias Could Borrow From GTA 6

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1612 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dualshockers

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As someone who usually writes about Metroidvanias but has recently been engrossed in GTA 6, I haven't stopped thinking about the points where the two converge.
  • Rockstar's fresh work isn't an adventure like the series' previous iterations; instead, it boasts an even finer and more meticulous design that, at fleeting moments, makes me feel it hides lessons beyond the obvious.
  • That games in its genre will follow in its footsteps is logical, but I truly believe there's a sufficiently diverse level of excellence to consider that not only open-world titles will benefit from its influence.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As someone who usually writes about Metroidvanias but has recently been engrossed in GTA 6, I haven't stopped thinking about the points where the two converge.

Rockstar's fresh work isn't an adventure like the series' previous iterations; instead, it boasts an even finer and more meticulous design that, at fleeting moments, makes me feel it hides lessons beyond the obvious.

That games in its genre will follow in its footsteps is logical, but I truly believe there's a sufficiently diverse level of excellence to consider that not only open-world titles will benefit from its influence.

Therefore, in order to return to writing about the type of games I'm passionate about while still fulfilling my communicative responsibility towards the interactive entertainment industry's latest titan, here are ten elements Metroidvanias could borrow from GTA 6.

Throughout its history, Grand Theft Auto has been a franchise of journeys, stories, and mechanics that unfold along the way rather than at the destination, giving vehicles a prominent role as in GTA 6.

In contrast, movement in Metroidvanias, despite the notable importance of exploration, is reduced to the characters and their abilities, limiting the worlds' scale to the equally slow speed at which their protagonists move.

Therefore, as the final stages of each campaign approach, fast travel becomes the key to backtracking, so the presence of manually controllable means of transport would not only add another layer of depth but also enable even larger worlds.

It doesn't have to be permanent, of course, as I personally love concrete maps that you can traverse on foot, yet the genre would benefit from a broader understanding of distance than it has been done so far.

Although I don't believe every game should have a plethora of minigames and side activities like GTA 6, I do think they highlight the narrow imagination with which Metroidvanias approach their gameplay concepts.

Speaking of verbs, fighting and moving are the only ones that can be attributed to their vast majority, instead of including more interactive elements that would help diversify the gaming experience.

Silver Pines, for example, does an excellent job in this regard by inheriting puzzles from horror games, but visual novels' decision-making, RPGs' morality systems, or stealth games' infiltrative sections could have a place in the right products.

Of course, it's easier to have diverse gameplay if you're an open-world game than if you're an action-adventure title, since the classification limits you, though I think it's a good time to break free from the shackles of labels.

Especially since FromSoftware's games have influenced the genre, it's become increasingly difficult to find a Metroidvania with a concrete story, told linearly and directly rather than through contextual and ambiguous elements.

These are rich and fertile narrative mechanisms for creating immersive worlds, no doubt, but the trope easily becomes exhausted after practically everyone resorts to it to tell their tales.

I'm not necessarily talking about cinematics or actors with impressive performances, but about campaigns with concrete beginnings, developments, and endings, as Prince of Persia: The Lost Crown and Ori and the Blind Forest have already done.

These examples demonstrate that it's achievable, and if we dare to go further and adopt a love story as emotional and sensitive as Jason and Lucia's, all the better.

Returning to the premise of gameplay variety, Metroidvanias have failed to convey the influence of their environments beyond the visual, as our ways of interacting with different biomes remain virtually unchanged.

You don't usually dive into aquatic biomes, just as you don't climb mountainous areas or sink into swamps, because the way we orient ourselves in space tends to be the same regardless of that location's unique characteristics.

In contrast, GTA 6 does a superb job of differentiating each of its regions, with activities adapted to the physical attributes of each one to truly convey the feeling that the world you're inhabiting exists.

I'm not suggesting the same level of depth or technological detail, but rather the same approach: to turn aesthetic beauty into playable immersion.

GTA 6, with its massive wardrobe and extensive customization system, reminded me of how special it felt to see Alucard's simple cape color change in Castlevania: Symphony of the Night depending on his equipment.

When you think of the greatest Metroidvanias, we all know and play the same protagonist, from their visual presentation to their gameplay styles, as the options are kept to a minimum to ensure precision and refinement.

It's a perfectly valid design sacrifice, and it has given us countless masterpieces, yet invalidating player expression by not allowing them to create their own unique gameplay and aesthetic combinations is a debt that has gone unpaid for years.

It's easier noted than done, considering how much more difficult it is to conceive of an avatar that offers so many alternatives, but it's so captivating in GTA 6 that I can't help but dream with the possibility.

Even with the perpetual satire and exaggeration inherent in GTA 6's story, it reminded me how unusual realistic narratives have become within the video game industry, which is at the mercy of various forms of fantasy instead.

Thus, would playing a Metroidvania governed by our universal laws be even remotely as entertaining as one with an entirely latest world? I don't have the slightest idea, precisely because this approach is so unexplored within the genre.

The conversations between Jason and Lucia feel so human, as do many of the events with NPCs and secondary characters, that you empathize almost instinctively, leading to a level of connection unusual in Metroidvanias.

Works like Shadow Complex or, to a lesser extent, Silver Pines itself, partially demonstrate this possibility, and I feel that exploring it would help open up a completely unique avenue for the genre, one that isn't limited to hand-drawn 2D side-scrollers.

Sources indicate that among the most striking aspects of GTA 6 is the way every NPC reacts to your every move. Whether it's walking, wearing unusual clothing, drawing a weapon, or saying something, there's an interaction waiting for you around every corner.

In the context of Metroidvanias, games like Hollow Knight have already explored the idea of characters responding to our actions, and even with the system's restrictions, it's an integral element of its worldbuilding.

Accordingly, building on that foundation and with an eye on Leonida's organic world, campaigns can be created where we feel our influence isn't rigidly predetermined but rather gradually constructed on both a macro and micro level.

It's difficult to anticipate the rapid arrival of a structure with such ramifications due to the predominance of independent developers in the genre, though simply having the horizon in sight is enough to begin moving towards it.

Ever since I played The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim, I've realized that progression in video games is almost always extradiegetic—that is, it happens before the player's eyes, not so much the character's—and GTA 6 also rejected this principle.

Consequently, "finding" a skill instead of developing it is a statement in itself about how a character grows, which is quite functional for the Metroidvania philosophy but not so much for the feeling of evolving through our gameplay experience.

I doubt it's interesting to lock the double jump behind having to go to the gym and do jumping jacks for a whole week, yet a game where our combat and movement skills expand based on how we interact with its base mechanics is a future that excites me.

GTA 6 makes it very simple, and sometimes it's even annoying, but the fact that it works here for the sake of realism doesn't mean that Metroidvanias can't use the same methodology for the sake of fun.

In Metroidvanias, there's no such thing as approaches: you either play the way the game wants you to, or you simply have to give up on the possibility of finishing it altogether.

GTA 6, inevitably, is also a slave to determinism, yet it leans slightly towards immersive sim design, allowing you to choose how you're going to fulfill your unchangeable obligations.

There are fights you can avoid with dialogue, wars you can replace with stealthy takedowns, and conflicts you can relocate with distraction tactics, thanks in part to a level design that offers more than one way to handle its execution.

I would never ask a Metroidvania to be Dishonored, though I could respectfully request that it at least try to integrate the possibility that not every challenge is solved by depleting a boss's health bar or completing an artificial platforming challenge.

I'd be lying if I didn't say I'm quite a fan of the true ending trope hidden behind an obscure side mission that unfolds outside the main campaign, but it does sadden me that it's the only option Metroidvanias often display.

While GTA 6 emphasizes numerous decisions, circumstances, and systems that occur at pivotal points in the plot and throughout the game, Metroidvanias have a much more reductive model.

Regardless of how you play, games in this genre tend to follow the formula of "good ending, bad ending by changing a decision before the final boss, true ending behind an optional mission", and it's starting to lose its appeal.

Certainly, GTA 6's approach isn't necessarily revolutionary or life-changing, yet it's complex enough to make you think about how you interact with its systems, so it more than achieves its goal.

Of course, for there to be impactful decisions to make, it's necessary to apply several of the fundamentals mentioned in this list, as they can't be achieved in isolation. However, since Rockstar's game will surely be the benchmark for many years to come, I'm sure some lessons will sink in.
